title: Find the Centre of the Star

concept.title: The centre of a star is the node that every edge touches
body: A **star graph** has one *centre* joined to every other node, and no other edges. It is the simplest shape with a "hub". The centre has degree `n - 1`; every other node has degree 1.

There are two easy ways to find the centre. One is to count the degrees and pick the node with degree `n - 1`. The other is to notice that **every edge contains the centre**: so the centre is the node that appears in both the first edge and the second edge. Only two edges are needed, because two different edges of a star share exactly the centre.

body.code:
a, b = edges[0]
c, d = edges[1]
centre = a if a == c or a == d else b

body: This is a tiny example of the way graph problems are often solved by a **structural property** (here: the centre lies on every edge), without any search. The condition `n >= 3` avoids the case of a single edge, where both ends would be a valid "centre".

statement: The graph with `n` nodes and `n - 1` edges is a star: one node (the centre) is joined to each of the other nodes, and there are no other edges. Print the centre.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
outputFormat: Print the number of the centre.
constraints: The graph is a star: one node, the centre, is joined to each of the other nodes, and there are no other edges.

examples.note: Node 4 is in all four edges.

hints: The centre belongs to every edge.
Look at the first two edges: they share exactly one node.
Or count the degrees and take the node with degree n - 1.

solution.complexity: Time O(1) after reading the input, space O(1).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

a, b = edges[0]
c, d = edges[1]
print(a if a == c or a == d else b)
